_comment: Short articles about changes and news on the network. `official` is maintainer-written; `community` is published from submissions the same way ideas are — nothing reaches either file automatically. An `image` is optional: `src` is a path under media/updates/, `alt` describes it for anyone who cannot see it, `focus` is a CSS object-position keeping the important part in frame when the card crops it, and `credit` names whoever the photograph belongs to. Do not publish a third-party photograph without a credit and the right to use it.

updates.title: Single fares drop to £2 in January
updates.summary: The national cap on a single bus fare falls from £3 to £2 from 1 January 2027.

image.alt: The destination display on the front of a double-decker bus reading “£2 Fare Cap”.
image.credit_note: Source and permission not recorded. Needs the site owner to confirm where this came from and on what terms, or to be replaced. Not invented here: an attribution that is guessed is worse than one that is missing.

updates.body:
It matters more here than the headline suggests. Crossing the Worthing/Brighton DayRider boundary does not by itself require two buses — the 700 runs straight through it — but a ticket boundary is where the day-ticket options stop covering you, so the fare cap is what keeps that journey at £6 return today and £4 from January. That is cheaper than every day ticket covering the same trip, which tells you something about how those zones are drawn.

Where two buses genuinely are needed — Lancing to Brighton, say — it is two singles each way: £12 return today, £8 once the cap drops.

The Ticket view journey checker prices singles alongside day tickets, so you can see which is actually cheaper for a given trip.

updates.title: Stagecoach moves to Ticketer — the same system B&H already runs
updates.summary: From September both major operators on this coast will be running the same ticketing platform, which removes the technical excuse for not accepting each other's tickets.

image.alt: A contactless bank card held against a blue Ticketer reader on a bus, the driver’s console display above it reading “Ticketer smart ticketing”.
image.credit_note: Source and permission not recorded. Needs the site owner to confirm where this came from and on what terms, or to be replaced. Not invented here: an attribution that is guessed is worse than one that is missing.

updates.body:
Stagecoach has appointed Ticketer as its supplier of ticketing and real-time information technology, deploying the detachable TK300 ticket machine across its fleet. The national rollout begins in September. The platform combines electronic ticketing, vehicle location and real-time information in one system.

Every Brighton & Hove bus already runs Ticketer. So from September, the two operators either side of the Shoreham boundary will be issuing and reading tickets on the same equipment, from the same supplier.

What this changes is the strength of one argument, not the state of the network. Mutual ticket acceptance has always carried a technical objection: two different ticketing systems, two sets of hardware. A shared supplier makes that objection harder to sustain.

It does not by itself make acceptance possible. A rollout beginning in September is not the same as local completion, and common equipment is not the same as interoperable products or an agreed way of splitting the revenue between operators. Those are commercial decisions, and nobody has announced them. We are asking for them; we are not reporting them as done.
